rationale: Biological visual sensitivity is not uniformly distributed across channels; melanopsin contributes to contrast-related processing.
Retinal gain changes with neuromodulatory/circadian state, supporting state-dependent sensing allocation.
Retinal resources are spatially partitioned according to distinct viewing environments.
Different eye types partition visual functions across distributed sensing channels.
Spatial information emerges from distributed receptors plus local optical screening.
Coarse vision can emerge from distributed body-level sensing and screening.
Dragonfly compound eyes allocate disproportionate sensor area and optical resolution to behaviorally relevant foveae and narrow visual bands rather than sampling space uniformly.
Asynchronous event sensing allocates processing to temporal change rather than uniformly sampled frames.
Active illumination redistributes event density to remain within finite sensor bandwidth.
Optical modulation can actively shape when and where event information is generated before reconstruction.
Stomatopods actively rotate sensing orientation to increase polarization contrast, showing that sensor geometry can be a controlled sensing variable.
Task-directed spatial guidance outperformed descriptive scene output for object reaching, supporting task utility as an explicit allocation objective.
Both vary effective sensing gain/allocation according to system state or load; biological and engineered mechanisms remain distinct.
Both allocate sensing resources non-uniformly across the available visual domain.
Both use optical modulation/screening before downstream interpretation to make spatial information recoverable; this is a functional analogy, not homology.
Distributed sensing plus constrained sampling illustrates information emerging under nonuniform spatial/temporal allocation.

Both close a perception-action loop by changing sensing behavior or guidance according to task-relevant spatial information; biological polarization alignment and digital reaching guidance remain mechanistically distinct.
Biological partitioning across optical domains supported the original distributed-function concept, but not enough to retain it as a standalone module.
Discrete optical focal states implement engineered partitioning of viewing conditions.
Continuous/angular light-field control extends the engineered side beyond discrete focus states.
Subclinical structural/electrophysiological changes motivate multimodal retinal measurement.
Adaptive-optics OCT increases retinal spatial/temporal observability.
Acquisition-side PSF engineering further improves cellular-scale retinal observability.
Phase diversity adds a computational restoration layer that estimates residual aberration while preserving acquisition hardware, making raw-versus-restored observability explicitly testable.
Early/subtle retinal change requires measurements whose acquisition and processing provenance can be separated from the biological signal; this links measurement architecture, not disease mechanism.
Subjective visual effects can dissociate from a conventional psychophysical endpoint.
Persistent subjective visual phenomena coexist with normal results on several basic measures.
Strong nonlinear optical visual phenomenon without sufficient current cross-front convergence.
Distributed photoreception plus screening can generate spatial vision.
Body-level screening and distributed receptors support coarse spatial vision.
Adaptive Visual Sampling is the sensing-policy component of the final MAXINE architecture.
Retinal Measurement Stack supplies the provenance and observability-integrity component of the final MAXINE architecture.
Verified focal/light-field state control is retained as an optional acquisition operator rather than a separate module.
Its distributed sensing and optical-screening principle is already represented inside the adaptive sensing architecture.
The measurement stack must preserve subjective/perceptual and objective structural/electrophysiological variables as distinct observables rather than treating one as a proxy for the other.
